findings.message: The update transaction sequences `npm ci` (Step 5) and the Verify check (Step 6) BEFORE the Auto-restore of local edits (Step 7). Because `npm ci` wipes `node_modules` and reinstalls only the shipped dependencies, any local edits that rely on custom dependencies will break after Step 7 restores them. The verify step passes on the stock vN+1 tree, but the instance subsequently terminates in a broken state post-restore. This violates the explicit promise that the instance 'ALWAYS terminates in a working state' and forces verification to run on the final assembled tree, not the intermediate pristine one.

The partial-failure rollback logic relies on re-running `npm ci` against the vN lockfile if Step 5 fails. Since Step 5 primarily fails due to network outages, the rollback's subsequent network fetch will likely also fail. Because `npm ci` deletes the existing `node_modules` folder prior to installation, a failed rollback leaves the tree with no dependencies. The user is falsely told the instance is 'back on vN, working', while it is actually unbootable. To safely handle interrupted-resume cases, the transaction must back up the existing `node_modules` folder (e.g., via rename) before fetching, rather than relying on a second network call during rollback.

The update transaction assumes all operator edits remain as uncommitted working tree changes that can be auto-stashed. If a collaborator commits their local edits to the release branch (a standard developer action), the `git merge --ff-only origin/release` step will permanently fail due to diverged history. The engine provides no auto-remediation for this state, explicitly violating the 'zero operator-typed git commands after first contact' success criterion by forcing the user to perform a manual git reset or rebase to fix their branch.

Phase 2 correctly builds a strict Node.js rename retry bound to mitigate Windows AV file-locking contention. However, Phase 4 delegates tree mutation to external `git merge` and `git stash` binaries. Git does not use the Phase 2 Node.js retry logic; if Windows AV or Search holds a lock on a file during the update, Git will fail immediately with an access error. The plan falsely assumes a clean tree guarantees a successful git merge on Windows. This bypasses the durability engineering introduced in Phase 2, creating a brittle update path that will spuriously fail and potentially leave the tree in a torn state mid-merge.

findings.section: Phase 3 — Default-Deny Security Model and Zero-Friction Token
findings.message: Writing an HTML file to disk and opening it in the default browser is a fragile bootstrap path. Many browser extensions (AV scanners, link previewers, ad blockers) proactively read local file contents or aggressively pre-fetch URLs found in them. Because the claim grant is single-use, if an extension pre-fetches the `127.0.0.1:<port>/claim` URL with the payload before the actual page script executes, the grant is consumed in the background. The user's actual browser tab will then fail to authenticate, breaking the 'working instance' promise and requiring manual intervention or restarts.

findings.section: Phase 3 — Default-Deny Security Model and Zero-Friction Token
findings.message: The exposure matrix allows `--i-understand-exposure` with a self-signed TLS cert and prints the fingerprint for 'out-of-band pinning'. However, modern web browsers have no UI to manually pin a certificate fingerprint. A collaborator connecting remotely will simply click 'Proceed to unsafe' to bypass the browser warning, meaning they will unknowingly accept a Man-in-the-Middle's certificate. They will then type the 10-minute pairing code into the MitM's page, allowing the attacker to intercept the code and instantly steal the session cookie. This violates the 'safe to expose' mandate.

findings.section: Phase 4 — Deny-by-Default Bundle Builder, Scrubbed Release Topology, and the Update Transaction
findings.message: The auto-update transaction assumes `git merge --ff-only origin/release` will always succeed on a tree that has been auto-stashed. This is false. If the collaborator locally commits a change instead of leaving it in the working tree, their local `release` branch will diverge from `origin/release`. The `ff-only` merge will fail, the transaction will rollback, and the collaborator will be permanently stuck on vN. They will be forced to manually run `git reset --hard` or `git rebase` to un-brick the update path, explicitly violating the 'zero operator-typed git commands after first contact' North Star criterion.

findings.section: Phase 7 — Release Integrity, the First-Contact Trust Anchor, and the External Red-Team Gate
findings.message: The threat model explicitly assumes the repo (including its docs) is attacker-controlled at clone time. If the out-of-band channel only delivers the three values (key fingerprint, tag name, commit hash) but relies on the repo's own `README.md` to provide the `git verify-commit` instructions, the attacker will simply rewrite `README.md` to omit the ceremony and instruct the user to run `anchor onboard` directly. The out-of-band communication MUST include the exact shell commands for the ceremony, not just the values, otherwise the trust anchor is bypassed trivially.

The zero-friction token bootstrap relies on a `file://` HTML page making a POST to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/claim` via an inline script. However, the plan states 'CORS disabled (no cross-origin responses at all)'. Modern browsers will block a cross-origin scripted POST from `file://` to `http://127.0.0.1` unless the server explicitly responds with CORS headers (e.g., `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null`) during the preflight or simple request. Disabling CORS entirely will cause the browser to silently block the claim POST, breaking the interactive onboarding path.

The partial-failure rollback for the update transaction specifies 'reset to the recorded vN SHA + npm ci against the vN lockfile'. Because `npm ci` deletes the `node_modules` directory before fetching, if the forward update failed due to network unavailability or an npm registry outage, the rollback's `npm ci` will fail for the exact same reason. This leaves the instance with a broken or missing `node_modules` directory and no network to fix it, violating the 'instance ALWAYS terminates in a working state' guarantee. Rollbacks must rely on local state (e.g., renaming the old `node_modules` before the update).

The auto-stash step uses `git status --porcelain` to find untracked files and move them aside so `git merge --ff-only` succeeds. Standard `--porcelain` omits `.gitignore`d files. If an incoming release introduces a file that the collaborator has locally as an ignored file, the merge will hard-abort with an 'untracked working tree files would be overwritten' error because auto-stash didn't see or move it. This forces the operator to manually intervene with git, breaking the 'zero operator-typed git commands' promise. Auto-stash must explicitly scan for and handle ignored files (e.g., via `git status --ignored`).
